title: Minstrel-era racial terms and insults
summary: Carew and the interviewers on how racial terms were used among minstrels and comedians, and a bus anecdote.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: All this business, you're talking about the thing of the nigger blues. You know, didn't you, the term nigger did not used to be derogatory at all. No. Back in the old days.

Well, in the old days, they were Negro minstrels and used it freely among themselves, back and forth. It was common with them, too, you see. That's right. That's the idea of there. The whole thing, the whole attitude was different, for instance. Now, they would get up. I saw Williams and Walker before they ever hit Broadway. And they were, Williams was the dumb Negro, and Walker was the flashy, smart Negro, kidding back and forth, you know. And, of course, if you want to take literally the gags, they passed back and forth. That's why they were insulting each other, you may say. And nobody thought anything of it. And the white comedians did the same thing, see. That's right. Not only in the Dutch, Dutch comedians, Irish comedians, Jewish comedians, Italian comedians. They roasted the life out of each other.

And that's what they do. They still wouldn't be doing today that's what they do. They didn't get into all this stuff. Well, they... I got to talking to Cliff about that one time. He said, oh, no, that's what they don't. He says, you can insult a man anytime you want to. You can tell. I don't care how you call it or how you pronounce it. He says, I know what you mean. Sure. And if you mean to insult me, you can call me until you want it.
Well, of course, a lot of those insults were terms of endearment.

Sure. There you go. I was on a bus one night sitting in the back end, and there were a lot of women on there and everything that's coming over from Rhode Island Avenue. We just about go up the hill. The guy got on there at the bottom of the hill coming over. He was from down here in the country somewhere. And he got on, he recognized the dry room. He said, well, so-and-so, what are you doing here? Why, you old son of a bitch, he says. I know. And he slapped him on. And he cut the-
And everybody- Everybody sat still. Sounded all right.
I know the women were shocked, but he was a good old friend of his. He's glad to see. Moses. Yeah, well, that's- But as you get educated, things change.
Maybe so. Let's see. Sometimes it don't change.
